text: Introgression between invasive and native blue mussels (genus Mytilus) in the central California hybrid zone. The ecological and genetic factors determining the extent of introgression between species in secondary contact zones remain poorly understood. Here, we investigate the relative importance of isolating barriers and the demographic expansion of invasive Mytilus galloprovincialis on the magnitude and the direction of introgression with the native Mytilus trossulus in a hybrid zone in central California. We use double-digest restriction-site-associated DNA sequencing (ddRADseq) to genotype 1337 randomly selected single nucleotide polymorphisms and accurately distinguish early and advanced generation hybrids for the first time in the central California Mytilus spp. hybrid zone. Weak levels of introgression were observed in both directions but were slightly more prevalent from the native M. trossulus into the invasive M. galloprovincialis. Few early and advanced backcrossed individuals were observed across the hybrid zone confirming the presence of strong barriers to interbreeding. Heterogeneous patterns of admixture across the zone of contact were consistent with the colonization history of M. galloprovincialis with more extensive introgression in northern localities furthest away from the putative site of introduction in southern California. These observations reinforce the importance of dynamic spatial and demographic expansions in determining patterns of introgression between close congeners, even in those with high dispersal potential and well-developed reproductive barriers. Our results suggest that the threat posed by invasive M. galloprovincialis is more ecological than genetic as it has displaced, and continues to displace the native M. trossulus from much of central and southern California.

Keywords: conservation genetics, hybridization, introgression, invasive species, molluscs, Mytilus Received 15 October 2014; revision received 28 July 2015; accepted 29 July 2015 Species introductions are a major threat to biodiversity (Vitousek et al. 1996; Mooney & Cleland 2001; Petit 2004) and are predicted to continue at an accelerating rate due to increases in human movement, direct ecosystem disturbance, modified reproductive phenology and increased abiotic stress induced by climate change (Mooney & Cleland 2001; Occhipinti-Ambrogi 2007; Hellmann et al. 2008). However, little is known about the genetic and ecological factors that allow intro- duced species to invade and displace native species. There is some evidence that introduced species coming in contact with closely related native species have a higher likelihood of successful naturalization (Daehler 2001; Diez et al. 2009; Jiang et al. 2010; Thuiller et al. 2010) and, as a consequence, are also more likely to hybridize. Therefore, hybridization and introgression might represent important risks associated with invasive species and understanding the mechanisms determining their importance becomes necessary for the successful management of biological invasions.

Introgression has long been appreciated as an important agent of evolutionary change (Anderson 1949; Barton 2001). Introgression can transfer adaptive Correspondence: Norah P. Saarman, Fax: (203) 432-5176; Molecular Ecology (2015) 24, 4723–4738 doi: 10.1111/mec.13340 alleles between species (Lewontin & Birch 1966; The Heliconius Genome Consortium 2012), supply additive genetic variance to facilitate phenotypic change (Grant & Grant 2008) or provide novel sources of genetic variation to colonizing species (Suarez & Tsutsui 2008). It may also circumvent evolutionary arms races such as host–pathogen interactions and sexual conflict (e.g. mussels in France, Boon et al. 2009; elms in Italy, Brunet et al. 2013), cause genetic pollution of a local species (Laikre et al. 2010) or influence the outcome of speciation (Nikula et al. 2008; Abbott et al. 2013). Despite the recognized importance of introgression, the pre- and postzygotic factors determining movement of genes between species are unpredictable and complicated by the difficulty of distinguishing introgression from incomplete lineage sorting (ILS). Both introgression and ILS result in the sharing of alleles between species and are heterogeneous across the genome (Tajima 1983; Barton & Hewitt 1985; Hudson & Coyne 2002). The fitness of hybrids and their ability to backcross with parental species and patterns of dispersal can lead to the extensive introgression of neutral alleles from a native species into an invasive congener under a broad range of conditions (Currat et al. 2008; Although introgression into the invasive species should be weak when intraspecific gene flow is high (Currat et al. 2008), this has not been tested for in high geneflow marine species that possess long pelagic larval periods and high dispersal potential. Marine mussels belonging to the genus Mytilus provide an excellent system to investigate the patterns of genomewide introgression associated with biological invasions. Three species belonging to the so-called blue mussel complex (Mytilus edulis, Mytilus trossulus and Mytilus galloprovincialis) exhibit strong, yet incomplete, reproductive barriers and have established both recent and ancient secondary contact zones across the world (Seed 1992; Lockwood & Somero 2011). The mosaic hybrid zone between M. galloprovincailis and M. edulis in western Europe formed following the last glacial cycle, but the timing of the secondary contact between these species has been recently estimated at ~700 000 years ago (Roux et al. 2014). The age of the hybrid zones between M. edulis and M. trossulus in the Baltic and the northwest Atlantic is also estimated at a comparatively deep age of ~7500 and 18 000 years ago, respectively (Riginos & Cunningham 2005; Rawson & Harper 2009). In contrast, the secondary contact and hybridization between M. galloprovincialis and M. trossulus in Japan (Inoue et al. 1995, 1997), central California (Suchanek et al. 1997) and Puget Sound (Heath et al. 1995) has occurred in the last several hundred years due to anthropogenic activities. The recent contact between M. galloprovincialis and M. trossulus, which diverged ~3.5 Ma (Seed 1992), provides an opportunity to study the patterns of hybridization and introgression during the initial period of invasion and range expansion and allows comparisons between hybrid zones of greater antiquity. The objective of this study was to examine the genomewide patterns of introgression between invasive M. galloprovincialis and native M. trossulus across their zone of hybridization in central California. As its introduction to southern California in the early 1900s, M. galloprovincialis has expanded northward and displaced M. trossulus from the southern part of its native range (Rawson et al. 1996, 1999; Geller 1999; Braby & Somero 2005; Lockwood & Somero 2011). Theory predicts that the rapid northward population expansion of M. galloprovincialis into coastal regions containing native M. trossulus should produce asymmetric introgression of genes into the invading species (Buggs 2007; Currat et al. 2008). Previous work in central California has suggested the genetic integrity of M. trossulus might be protected from introgression from M. galloprovincialis by selection associated with local environmental conditions (Braby & Somero 2005). However, earlier studies have used a small number of diagnostic markers that are incapable of accurately identifying advanced hybrids or backcrosses. By incorporating a large number of randomly selected SNPs, our study provides the first clear genomewide patterns of introgression between a pair of Mytilus congeners, and allows us to assess the relative contributions of colonization history and range expansion.

We sampled an average of 28 individuals from each of seven localities within the California M. galloprovincialis and M. trossulus hybrid zone (one site was sampled twice). Twenty-two individuals were sampled from two putatively pure populations from outside the hybrid zone (Newport Harbor, OR, USA and Santa Barbara, CA, USA) and six M. galloprovincialis were obtained from its native range in France (Sete), providing a total sample of 26 M. galloprovincialis (Fig. 1). Samples were collected between July 2010 and 2012. Most animals were collected in the summer of 2010 with the exception of Tiburon Point, which was sampled both in 2010 and in 2012; Oakland (Lake Merritt) and Sete, which were sampled in 2011; and San Rafael Bridge and Carquinez Strait, which were sampled in 2012 (Table 1). DNA was extracted from gill tissue preserved in 100% ethanol and stored at 20 °C using a DNAeasy Blood 4724 N. P. SAARMAN and G. H. POGSON and Tissue kit (Qiagen, Valencia, CA, USA). DNA was quantified using a Qubit 2.0 Fluorometer (Life Technologies, Grand Island, NY, USA). Restriction-site-associated DNA libraries were prepared following the protocol of Peterson et al. (2012) with slight modifications to account for the Mytilus spp. genome size and high polymorphism (Rodriquez-Juiz et al. 1996; Cruz et al. 2005; Saavedra & Bachere 2006) using restriction enzymes SphI-HF and MluCI (see Supporting information for details). Forty-eight or 60 individuals were pooled per library (i.e. fewer individuals were pooled for the de novo library to ensure adequate coverage) and sent to the QB3 Vincent J. Coates Genomics Sequencing Laboratory at UC Berkeley for 50 bp singleread Library Sequencing on the HiSeq2000 platform (Illumina, San Diego, CA, USA).

Forty-eight individuals were used in an initial run to determine the appropriate ddRADseq tag length (in bp) and identify orthologous tags present in both M. trossulus and M. galloprovincialis. We took extra precaution with these samples to ensure the reference catalog of SNPs used in this study were of Mytilus spp. origin. The 48 individuals used for the de novo library were kept in filtered flowing sea water for a minimum of 1 week before DNA extractions. We chose a trim length of 35 bp as our parental catalog because this represented the largest number of usable SNPs [without the risk of misidentifying homologous reads due to insufficient read length (see Fig. S1 and Supporting information for details)]. We discarded Casava ‘filtered’ flagged reads using the fastq_illumina_filter (http://cancan.cshl.edu/ labmembers/gordon/fastq_illumina_filter) and demultiplexed using the unique P1 barcodes with Sabre (https://github.com/najoshi/sabre). An additional 5 bp was trimmed from both the 50 and 30 end of each read, with the final read length standardized to 35 bp, and applied another quality filter (Phred score >20) with a custom Python wrapper and Sickle (https://github.- com/najoshi/sickle). The results were visualized with FastQC (Andrews 2010).

Moss Landing 36.804°, 121.786° 25 2010 Demultiplexed, quality-filtered and trimmed reads from all 276 individuals (35 bp in length) were aligned into exactly matching ‘stacks’ using ustacks in the STACKS v.1.03 pipeline (Catchen et al. 2011, 2013) with parameters d r m 6 M 3. The reads were matched against a parental catalog of M. trossulus and M. galloprovincialis de novo assembly catalog of consensus ‘stacks’ built from samples of pure species, also using the STACKS pipeline (see Supporting information for details). These settings removed highly repetitive stacks (lumberjack stacks) and stacks with unlikely genotype frequencies while maintaining a minimum coverage of 69. To obtain a subset of SNPs present in both species, we used the populations.pl script from the STACKS pipeline to filter SNPs scored in at least 75% of samples (parameter r 0.75) yielding a total of 1337 SNPs.

We performed a reciprocal discontinuous search using the stand-alone NCBI search tool MEGABLAST (Zhang et al. 2000) with the de novo assembly catalog of consensus ‘stacks’ as the query and a Sanger sequenced expressed sequence tag (EST) library from Mytilus californianus as the subject Lockwood and colleagues kindly provided the M. californianus 13 082 gene EST library in a refined format that included only unique single-copy coding genes as determined by the PartiGene bioinformatics pipeline (Parkinson et al. 2004; Lockwood et al. 2010). We only considered matches that had e-value thresholds <1E-10, identity matches >90% and lengths >30 bp. This provided a conservative identification of SNPs within exons of single-copy coding genes.

We used STRUCTURE v2.3.4 (Pritchard et al. 2000; Falush et al. 2003, 2007), the R package INTROGRESS v1.22 (Gompert & Buerkle 2010) and NEWHYBRIDS v1 (Anderson & Thompson 2002; Anderson 2008) to identify pure species and hybrids and to classify hybrids into categories (i.e. F1, F2, backcross with M. galloprovincialis, or backcross with M. trossulus). STRUCTURE jointly assigns individuals probabilistically to the two parental classes without prior input. STRUCTURE analyses used all 1337 SNPs that passed our primary filters. We used a burn in of 50 000 sweeps and then ran 100 000 sweeps in five separate runs checking for convergence of the estimated membership coefficient (Q) across runs. NEWHYBRIDS analyses included only diagnostic SNPs, Jeffreys-type priors, and a burn in of 10 000 sweeps followed by 50 000 sweeps in five separate runs. Convergence of Q across runs was again checked. We also performed a principle components analysis with the ‘ADEGENET’ package version 1.4-2 (Jombart 2008) in the R version 3.1.0 environment (R Core Team, 2013). Genome-wide estimates of admixture were performed with INTROGRESS, an R package that makes a maximumlikelihood estimate of the ancestry of each individual. Ancestry can be summarized in a hybrid index, which is an estimation of the proportion of alleles inherited from one of two hybridizing parental species. The results from the PCA were used to inform a priori definitions of parental genotypes. We defined parent species 1 (M. trossulus) as any animal from Newport Harbor that fell in the low 20% of principle component 1 (PC 1), and parental species 2 (M. galloprovincialis) as any animal from France or from Santa Barbara that fell in the top 20% of PC 1. We also identified diagnostic fixed SNPs with INTROGRESS, which estimates interspecific delta allele frequency per locus.

Linkage disequilibrium (LD) between all pairs of loci and heterozygote deficiency relative to Hardy–Weinberg (HW) proportions (using FIS values) was tested for all loci with corrections for finite populations (Kirby 1975; Nei 1977) using the GENETICS package version (Warnes et al. 2013) in the R environment. One hundred and thirty-two markers were excluded from all tests for LD and HWD because they were tri-allelic (typically with one of the alleles at very low frequency). The large number of tri-allelic loci in this data set is likely a consequence of high polymorphism in bivalves. We made separate estimates for M. trossulus from Newport Harbor, all mussels from Newport Harbor, a pooled hybrid zone sample, and all individuals from Santa Barbara. Only 566 and 414 of the 1337 SNPs genotyped could be included in tests for LD and HWD in pure M. trossulus and pure M. galloprovincialis, respectively, because the majority were missing the homozygote genotype of the opposite genetic background.

Population structure of colonizing Mytilus galloprovincialis To obtain a subset of SNPs informative in population genetics comparison of M. galloprovincialis, we used the populations.pl script from the STACKS pipeline to filter SNPs scored in at least 75% of samples from individuals identified as M. galloprovincialis, which yielded a 4726 N. P. SAARMAN and G. H. POGSON total of 7820 ‘stacks’ with 19 212 variant sites. Sample sizes were variable because they depended on STRUCTURE assignment (Fig. 2). We standardized sample sizes to 22 individuals from Bodega Bay, Berkeley, Oakland and Santa Barbara, 15 individuals from Moss Landing, and six individuals from Sete, France. The populations.pl script provided population-specific counts of private alleles, observed and expected heterozygosities, nucleotide diversity and FIS measures and pairwise estimates of FST. We also randomly subsampled six individuals from each population to match the sample size of Sete and reran the populations.pl script to obtain comparable estimates of private alleles and FST. Correlations between PC 1 and the distance in kilometre from the putative site of introduction (i.e. the Port of Los Angeles) were tested with a linear regression in JMP version 10.0.2 (SAS Institute Inc, Rockville, MD, USA). We included Santa Barbara and all localities within the hybrid zone and any individual classified by NEWHYBRIDS as pure M. galloprovincialis, M. galloprovincialis backcross, or as advanced generation hybrids. We reran the analysis excluding Bodega Bay and Oakland because of the possibility that M. galloprovincialis in these localities result from more recent direct human introductions.

We employed the genomic clines method of Gompert & Buerkle (2010) in INTROGRESS, which has its origins in Barton’s concordance analysis (Szymura & Barton 1986). This method compares admixture at a single locus to average admixture across the rest of the genome. We used the parametric approach, first estimating a multilocus hybrid index and then fitting clines in genotype frequencies at individual SNPs as a function of the neutral expectation derived from the genomewide hybrid index. Although the parametric approach is preferred when parental populations do not exhibit fixed differences for alleles at all of the assayed molecular markers (Gompert & Buerkle 2010), it has a higher false discovery rate than the alternative method. We interpreted any significant deviation in the probabilities of an individual genotype as moderate asymmetry (scored 1 or 1 depending on direction), and an overall significant deviation for all three genotypes at a locus as substantial asymmetry (scored 2 or 2), and used these values to test for heterogeneity with a nested analysis of variance.

The final data set included 562 million high-quality reads. On average, ~2.43 [standard deviation (SD) 1.31] million reads beginning with the correct restriction-siteassociated sequence were obtained per individual. Of ~1.20 million SNPs present from each parental species, 17 102 were polymorphic with 1–4 SNPs at a trim length of 35 bp. The BluePippin size selection system was somewhat inconsistent, resulting in overlap of only 1337 SNPs across all populations that passed filtering criteria and only 211 (15.78%) were identified as species-specific fixed diagnostic markers (Fig. S1, Supporting information). There was a paucity of SNPs with interspecific delta allele frequency between 0.7 and 1 (Fig. S2, Supporting information). Ten individuals scored for fewer than 25% of the SNPs were excluded from all subsequent analyses (Fig. S3, Supporting information). After all filtering steps, the SNPs had a mean coverage of 35.19 with moderate variance (SD 14.19 per individual, and SD 27.79 per SNP). Mean coverage per individual was strongly correlated with per cent SNPs successfully scored (Fig. S4, Supporting information), and hybrids had equal coverage to pure species (Supporting information).

The MEGABLAST search of ‘stacks’ against the Mytilus californianus EST library returned hits for 30 of the 1337 tags with polymorphic SNPs (Table S1, Supporting information) suggesting that only 2.2% of the restriction-siteassociated DNA fragments included in our final analyses fall within exons uninterrupted by introns or noncoding DNA. Five of the 211 diagnostic SNPs fell within coding regions (Table S1, Supporting information).

STRUCTURE and PCA yielded consistent results and were used to identify pure M. trossulus and M. galloprovincialis individuals from Newport Harbor and Santa Barbara for assignment of parental genotypes in subsequent analyses (Fig. 2). NEWHYBRIDS assignment of early generation hybrid categories detected 19 F1 hybrids, nine advanced generation hybrids (‘other hybrids’) and three first-generation backcrosses into M. galloprovincialis. No first-generation backcrosses into M. trossulus were observed. Because we used the default genotype frequency classes in the NEWHYBRIDS analysis, it is possible that backcrosses were misassigned as pure species. However, INTROGRESS results corroborated these findings by identifying few individuals with hybrid scores compatible with early generation backcrosses. Hybrid indices for all samples in the hybrid zone plotted against interspecific heterozygosity produced no hybrid scores between 0.1 and 0.4 (expected for early generation backcrosses into M. trossulus), and only four individuals had hybrid scores between 0.6 and 0.9 (consistent with early generation backcrosses into M. galloprovincialis), three of which were assigned backcross status, and the remaining individual originated from outside of the hybrid zone (Fig. 3). In contrast, there was an abundance of hybrid scores around 0.5 (F1 hybrids) and close to 0 (pure M. trossulus) or 1 (pure M. galloprovincialis) (Fig. 3). We observed substantial heterogeneity in the genetic composition between different sites and at the same site across years, which is consistent with earlier studies that used small numbers of markers (Sarver & Foltz 1993; Rawson et al. 1996, 1999; Suchanek et al. 1997; Braby & Somero 2005). For example, the percentage of M. galloprovincialis in samples from Berkeley was ~25% in the 1990s, ~60% in the 2000s and ~80% in the present study. In the San Rafael samples, M. galloprovincialis was present at ~25% in the 1990s, ~40% in the 2000s and only 2% in the present study (Fig. S5, Supporting information).

As expected, tests for LD identified a large number of SNPs with nonrandom associations and tests for HWD detected substantial numbers of SNPs with heterozygote deficiencies. At a 2% significance level, the pooled hybrid zone sample showed much higher incidence of LD and HWD (29.3% of SNP pairs in LD and 47.3% of SNPs in HWD) than pure M. trossulus or M. galloprovincialis samples (Table S2, Supporting information). Pure M. trossulus from Newport Harbor, OR, showed LD in as many as 1.6% of SNP pairs, and HWD in 0.8% of SNPs. A comparative sample of pure M. galloprovincialis from Santa Barbara showed LD in 1.0% of SNP pairs and HWD in 1.2% of SNPs (Table S2, Supporting information).

Population structure of colonizing Mytilus galloprovincialis Population-specific counts of private alleles were substantially higher in the Santa Barbara sample compared with other localities. The Santa Barbara sample contained 1899 private alleles in a sample of 22 individuals. Other samples of comparable size had between 291 and 359 private alleles. Randomly subsampling six individuals from each population (to match the Sete sample size) produced the same results with Santa Barbara having 916 private alleles compared with a range of 361– 502 for the others (Table 2). Observed and expected heterozygosities, nucleotide diversity and FIS measures all corroborate higher genetic diversity in Santa Barbara (Table 2). Pairwise estimates of FST revealed minimal population structure. All pairwise FST estimates comparing the Sete sample of M. galloprovincialis to California samples were nonsignificant and relatively homogenous (ranging from 0.021 to 0.037) with Moss Landing displaying the highest pairwise estimate (Table 2). However, we observed a significant correlation between PC 1 and distance from the Port of Los Angeles (r2 = 0.1677, With exclusion of Bodega Bay and Oakland (i.e. sites with risk of recent direct human introduction of M. galloprovincialis), correlation between PC 1 and distance from the Port of LA was even stronger (r2 = 0.2361; Pvalue < 0.0001).

Genomic clines exhibited substantial discordance across SNPs. In the pooled hybrid zone, 364 of 1337 SNPs (27.2%) display overall significant deviation from neutral expectations for all three genotypes at a locus. Considering only SNPs with high (>0.8) delta frequency between pure species, 158 of 301 (52.5%) showed significant deviations from the neutral expectations (Table S3, Supporting information). Deviations were observed in all possible combinations of deficits and excesses with minimal concordance across the entire hybrid zone. Only ~50% of the SNPs displaying neutral introgression in the pooled hybrid zone exhibited neutral patterns in all localities tested individually, and the nested analysis of variance indicates that Bodega Bay and Carquinez have more introgression of M. trossulus alleles than other localities and that Moss Landing has more introgression of M. galloprovincialis alleles (Fig. 5). SNPs with genomic clines deviating from the null expectation of equal admixture fell into several distinct categories. For the 301 SNPs with high (>0.8) delta frequency between pure species, only 62 (20.6%) consistently showed an excess of M. trossulus/M. trossulus (TT) genotypes with the exception of moderate asymmetry in the opposite direction in a maximum of one locality (always Moss Landing). These SNPs exhibited consistent steep genomic clines and had high probabilities of TT genotypes even at hybrid scores > 0.5. A total of 43 SNPs (14.3%) consistently showed the opposite pattern; M. galloprovincialis/M. galloprovincialis (gg) excess with the exception of moderate asymmetry in the opposite direction in a maximum of one locality (variable San Francisco Bay localities). The study of hybrid zones has long provided important insights into the evolution of pre- and postzygotic isolating barriers between divergent populations or species (Barton & Hewitt 1985; Harrison 1990; Coyne & Orr 2004). However, most hybrid zones studied to date are well established and thus provide little insight into the genetic consequences that occur during the initial phase of secondary contact. Our study investigated the genetic impact of an invasion by M. galloprovincialis into southern and central California that has displaced the native M. trossulus and resulted in the formation of a mosaic hybrid zone in the San Francisco Bay area (Rawson et al. 1996, 1999; Geller 1999; Braby & Somero 2005). We observed complex patterns of weak introgression across the hybrid zone suggesting strong selection against hybrids and the erratic population expansion of M. galloprovincialis have played important roles in shaping the genetic composition of mussel populations across this region.

Theory predicts that the rapid expansion of M. galloprovincialis into central California over the past century should result in asymmetrical introgression of neutral genes from the native M. trossulus into the invading species (Currat & Excoffier 2004; Currat et al. 2008), a pattern that has been reported in wide range of organisms (e.g. Gantenbein & Largiader 2002; Schierenbeck et al. 2005; Leache 2011; see review by Currat et al. 2008). Although we detected a higher level of introgression into the invading M. galloprovincialis than into the native M. trossulus (20.4% vs. 14.6% of SNPs, respectively), the degree of asymmetry was weak and few advanced backcrossed individuals were identified in the hybrid zone. This is most likely a consequence of strong and pervasive selection acting against F1 hybrids and backcrossed individuals. However, limited matings between species and high levels of gene flow in the invading species are expected to diminish the magnitude of asymmetry (Currat et al. 2008) and both may have been factors in our study. Furthermore, erratic and heterogeneous patterns of population expansion (Gaylord & Gaines 2000; Selkoe et al. 2006) or contraction (Hilbish et al. 2010) along the California coast may have weakened the signal of asymmetrical introgression. Indeed, significant differences in the direction of introgression were detected across the hybrid zone (Fig. with Bodega Bay and Carquinez showing more introgression from native M. trossulus into the invasive M. galloprovincialis, and Moss Landing showing more introgression from M. galloprovincialis into the native M. trossulus. Heterogeneous patterns of admixture have also been observed in large portions of the genomes in subspecies of Macoma balthica (Luttikhuizen et al. 2012) and Ciona intestinalis (Roux et al. 2013).

Previous studies on hybridization and introgression between M. trossulus and M. galloprovincialis used small numbers of diagnostic markers that severely limited their ability to identify advanced backcrosses (e.g. Rawson et al. 1999; Braby & Somero 2005; Brannock et al. 2009). Assuming that the 1337 SNPs scored in the present study were randomly distributed across the genomes of both species, each of the 14 Mytilus chromosomes is expected to have been marked by ~96 SNPs. With this genomewide perspective, we detected few first-generation (3) or advanced generation hybrid individuals (9), thus confirming the presence of strong reproductive barriers between species. Previous studies in other Mytilus spp. pairs have identified a variety of endogenous and exogenous isolating mechanisms. POGSON example, in M. edulis and M. galloprovincialis in Europe, researchers have found evidence of environmental selection mediated by salinity and wave exposure (reviewed by Gardner 1994), asynchronous spawning (Secor et al. 2001; Gilg et al. 2007), assortative fertilization success (Bierne et al. 2002), habitat choice (Bierne et al. 2003a) and the presence of large numbers of recessive Dobzhansky-Muller (DM) incompatibility loci across the genomes of both species (Bierne et al. 2006). Similarly, studies of M. edulis and M. trossulus in the Baltic Sea suggest strong reproductive isolation caused by a combination of exogenous and endogenous preand postzygotic factors (Riginos & Cunningham 2005; Zbawicka et al. 2014). The reproductive barriers between the subjects of this study, M. galloprovincialis and M. trossulus, have been the focus of far fewer studies. Spawning asynchrony has been observed between M. galloprovincialis and M. trossulus in the Pacific Northwest (Matson et al. 2003), but in San Francisco Bay, the two species have broadly overlapping periods of settlement (Braby & Somero 2005). Some role for habitat selection mediated by salinity and temperature has been suggested by Braby & Somero (2005) and Beaumont et al. (2005), but the patterns of introgression observed in the present study fail to exhibit any clear associations with variable environmental conditions. Over the past 20 years, the proportions of pure species and hybrids at various sites across the central California hybrid zone exhibit considerable spatial and temporal heterogeneity (Table S5, Supporting information) that is difficult to reconcile with environmentally mediated selection. Brannock & Hilbish (2010) observed that F1 hybrids between M. galloprovincialis and M. trossulus exhibited arrested gametogenesis, which they estimate would reduce their fertility by an order of magnitude. These observations suggest that endogenous barriers to introgression are far more important than exogenous barriers in maintaining species identities. In contrast to the strong postzygotic barriers, the detection of moderate numbers of F1 hybrids suggests that gametic isolation is weak. Previous studies have found that the proportion of F1 hybrids between these species can vary dramatically over small geographic scales. For example, Brannock et al. (2009) observed few F1 hybrids between M. galloprovincialis and M. trossulus along the northern side of Hokkaido, Japan but on the southern side the proportion of F1 hybrids at different sites commonly exceeded 50%. This variation in the proportion of F1 hybrids in Japan (and elsewhere) likely reflects differences in the opportunities for heterospecific matings because hybrid vigour has not been documented between M. galloprovincialis and M. trossulus (Matson et al. 2003). POGSON positive selection has acted at the sperm M7 lysin gene in Mytilus spp. (Riginos & McDonald 2003), most notably at two haplotype groups segregating in M. galloprovincialis (Riginos et al. 2006; Springer & Crespi 2007). The adaptive diversification of M7 lysin genes in mussels does not appear to greatly influence heterospecific fertilization success, which runs counter to the pattern expected by reinforcement selection in M. galloprovincialis (i.e. during secondary contact with M edulis).

High levels of linkage disequilibrium (LD) between SNPs and overall steep genomic clines (Fig. 6) further support our conclusion of restricted genetic exchange. With moderate to high levels of introgression, recombination will break down associations between markers and re-establish Hardy–Weinberg proportions and linkage equilibrium. It is worth noting, however, that a large number of chromosomal rearrangements have been described in Mytilus spp. (e.g., Ahmed & Sparks 1970; Insua et al. 1994) that could contribute to LD regardless of introgression levels (Strobeck 1983; Rieseberg 2001; Kirkpatrick & Barton 2006). The genomic clines observed in the present study are much steeper than those reported in other Mytilus spp. The M. edulis and M. galloprovincialis hybrid zone ‘HZ1’ and neighbouring pure populations in France shows a gradual genomic cline with individuals present at each hybrid score (Bierne et al. 2003b). A hybrid zone between M. edulis and M. trossulus in the Canadian Maritimes studied by Comesa~na et al. (1999), and in the Baltic Sea studied by Zbawicka et al. (2014) both exhibit more gradual genomic clines, and again, individuals were represented across the hybrid score index. The difference between the steep genomic cline in the present study and that in the Canadian and Baltic Sea hybrid zones cannot be explained by different levels of divergence between species because M. trossulus is equally related to M. galloprovincialis and M. edulis. It is more likely that the reduced level of backcrossing observed in our study reflects the short duration of secondary contact. The genomic clines analyses also revealed nonuniform patterns of introgression at a substantial number of SNPs. Overall, 364 of the 1337 SNPs (27.2%) and 158 of the 301 SNPs (52.5%) with frequency differences exceeding 0.80 between parental populations differed significantly from the neutral expectation (Table S3, Supporting information). These proportions are likely underestimated due to the limited statistical power produced by our small sample sizes. Non-neutral patterns are consistent with the presence of large numbers of DM incompatibility loci scattered across the genomes of both species. Our findings are similar to the hybrid zone formed between subspecies of Macoma. balthica in the Baltic Sea, where genomic cline analyses revealed 36.9% of polymorphic amplified fragment length polymorphisms behaved in a non-neutral manner (Luttikhuizen et al. 2012). It would be interesting to compare the results of the present study with similar genomewide analyses in hybrid zones between M. edulis and M. trossulus, and between M. edulis and M. galloprovincialis. Discrepancies between species-pair comparisons could provide insights into the evolution of lineage-specific barrier loci.

Introduction and spread of Mytilus galloprovincialis Even with limited introgression from M. trossulus, the northward expansion of M. galloprovincialis from southern California should produce a geographic pattern of increasing levels of admixture from the point of introduction (Currat et al. 2008). Excluding M. trossulus and hybrids from the data, we identified increasing introgression with distance from the presumed point of introduction in southern California (Fig. 4). Furthermore, we identified two sites in northern California (Bodega Bay and Oakland) with high abundances of M. galloprovincialis but low allelic diversity (Table 3), indicating few fully introgressed M. trossulus alleles. It is likely that the Bodega Bay sample has been impacted from aquaculture operations in the nearby Tomales Bay that farm M. galloprovincialis from hatchery-produced spat. The presence of pure M. galloprovincialis in Oakland is unexplained but might reflect an unauthorized transplantation or a recent new invasion. When the Bodega Bay and Oakland samples were excluded from the data, the introgression of M. trossulus alleles into M. galloprovincialis exhibits stronger correlation with distance from the presumed point of introduction in southern California (Fig. 4). This provides support for the introduction of M. galloprovincialis into southern California followed by a rapid range expansion and displacement of M. trossulus from southern California north to Monterey and San Francisco Bays.

Individuals identified as M. galloprovincialis in Santa Barbara exhibited a substantially higher allelic diversity than those sampled from other California localities (Table 3). As expected, the large pool of private SNP alleles observed in Santa Barbara did not contribute to differentiation among samples; pairwise FST-values between pure M. galloprovincialis from Sete and those sampled across California were uniform. It is possible that the large number of private alleles observed in Santa Barbara M. galloprovincialis has introgressed from M. trossulus. This is supported by the observation that ~12% of the SNPs that are diagnostic for M. galloprovincialis in Sete but variable in Santa Barbara are identical to the most common M. trossulus haplotypes across the entire ddRADseq tag and many of these alleles occur in a single individual (SAB07). It is unlikely artefacts of the ddRADseq method were responsible for this result because the numbers of sites sequenced per M. galloprovincialis sample was uniform (Table 3) and we applied rigorous quality control filters for all included reads.
Why is Mytilus galloprovincialis such a successful invader?

Previous studies have established that M. galloprovincialis is competitively dominant to M. edulis in Europe (reviewed by Gardner 1994). Mytilus galloprovincialis differs from other Mytilus species in having faster growth rates, earlier reproduction, a higher resistance to disease (Moore et al. 1991; Roch 1999; Bierne et al. 2003b; Barber 2004; Ciocan et al. 2006; Vassilenko & Baldwin 2014), a warmer thermal evolutionary history (Thunell 1979; Mann & Hamilton 1995) and greater resilience to heat stress (Geller 1999; Braby & Somero 2006; Lockwood et al. 2010; Tomanek & Zuzow 2010; Lockwood & Somero 2011). The rapid spread of M. galloprovincialis into central California suggests that it also has a fitness advantage over M. trossulus over a broad range of environmental conditions. However, it is possible that M. trossulus can outcompete M. galloprovincialis in habitats experiencing large annual fluctuations in salinity and temperature, such as the northern part of San Francisco Bay. Whether it can persist in isolated pockets indefinitely is unclear. It is now apparent that hybridization has played an important role in the evolution of invasiveness is plants (reviewed by Schierenbeck & Ellstrand 2009). The evidence for a similar role for hybridization in animals is far more limited. However, several recent studies have shown that introgression has resulted in the adaptive movement of genes between M. edulis and M. galloprovincialis in the European mosaic hybrid zone (e.g. Boon et al. 2009; Fra€ısse et al. 2014). We suggest that the acquisition of novel adaptive genes from M. edulis in Europe may have contributed to the invasive success of M. galloprovincialis into California and other parts of the world. Our study has clearly shown that M. galloprovincialis has acquired genetic material from M. trossulus as it invaded southern and central California. Although most genes entering M. galloprovincialis are likely deleterious, it is possible that some adaptive introgression is presently occurring that may facilitate its invasion potential. However, the threat posed by invasive M. galloprovincialis in California is more ecological than genetic (cf. Brannock & Hilbish 2010). The limited introgression from M. galloprovincialis into M. trossulus suggests that the native species is largely immune to genetic invasion and that the ecological consequences of being displaced from its original habitat is a far more serious threat to its persistence in central California.
